content: The earlobe, also known as the lobulus auriculae, is the soft, lower portion of the external ear in humans and many other animals. It is anatomically similar in composition to the labia or pinna. The earlobe is the lowermost part of the human pinna and extends below the antitragus. Unlike the rest of the pinna, the earlobe lacks cartilage, which accounts for its softness and lack of elasticity. It is primarily composed of tough areolar and adipose (fatty) connective tissues. The earlobe has a rich blood supply, which may contribute to warming the ears, but it is generally not considered to have any significant biological function. The average length of an earlobe is approximately 2 cm, and it tends to elongate slightly with age. Earlobes can be classified as either free (hanging freely from the head) or attached (connected directly to the head). This distinction is a classic example of simple genetic dominance. Freely hanging earlobes are associated with the dominant allele, while attached earlobes are linked to the recessive allele. Individuals with one dominant allele for free earlobes and one recessive allele for attached earlobes will exhibit the freely hanging earlobe trait. Statistically, free earlobes are twice as common in the human population as attached earlobes. Earlobes are typically smooth, but in some cases, they may exhibit creases. Creased earlobes have been associated with certain genetic disorders, such as Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome. Additionally, earlobe creases have been linked to an increased risk of heart attack and coronary heart disease. However, since earlobes tend to develop creases with age, and older individuals are more likely to experience heart disease, age may be a confounding factor in this association. The earlobe contains numerous nerve endings, making it a recognized erogenous zone. Throughout human history and across various cultures, the earlobe has been the most common site for body piercing. Tearing of the earlobe can occur due to the weight of heavy earrings or traumatic pulling of an earring, but such tears are generally straightforward to repair. Some cultures practice earlobe stretching, using piercing ornaments to gradually enlarge the earlobes. Earlobe piercings carry a significantly lower risk of infection compared to piercings in other parts of the ear. The initial healing period for an earlobe piercing typically lasts 6 to 8 weeks. After this time, earrings can be changed, but if the piercing is left unfilled for an extended period, there is a risk of the hole closing. Even after healing, earlobe piercings may shrink to smaller gauges if earrings are not worn for a prolonged period, but the piercing may never completely close.
